To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
human thymic epithelial cells and dendritic cells are susceptible to HIV-1 infection, and that the virus induces apoptosis in these cells.
HIV infection of human thymocytes results in the release of a factor(s) that kills uninfected thymocytes.
HIV-1 induces apoptosis in human thymocytes, and that this process is mediated by the production of a factor(s) by infected thymic dendrite cells (TDCs).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of HIV-induced cytotoxicity and its role in HIV-mediated pathogenesis.
the identification of the mechanisms involved in the HIV-induced CD4+ T-cell depletion.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms of HIV-1-induced CD4 T-cell death.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HIV-induced apoptosis of CD4+ lymphocytes is not the only cause of CD4+ cell death in HIV infection.
HIV-1 infection leads to an increased rate of apoptosis of CD4+ lymphocytes (8).
apoptosis is a major mechanism of CD4+ cell death, but it is not the only mechanism of CD4 + cell death (8).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV infection of human thymus results in the release of a factor that induces apoptosis in CD4+ T lymphocytes.
HIV-1 infection of human thymocytes leads to the release of a factor(s) that induces apoptotic death of uninfected cells.
HIV-1 infection of thymic DCs induces a cytotoxic factor release, and this release of the factor(s) induces the apoptosis of CD4+ cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the virus itself, in a cell-free form, can trigger cell death.
the thymus is a major site for HIV-1 infection and that thymic dendrite cells (DCs) play a key role in the pathogenesis of HIV-1 infection.
we have identified a novel mechanism by which HIV can induce apoptosis.
